But wait — the slide BFS's passable set includes 'c' (charcoal). The sprite's own cells are 'b' and 'c'. When the sprite occupies a cell, that cell is rendered as b/c instead of W/g. That's fine for box_ok (the sprite's own cells are passable).
Hmm, but the slide BFS found only 11 states. Let me look at the slide endpoints:
- (33,45): D → (33,45) (can't go down — B at rows 36-38, cols 45-47). L → (33,39) (can't go past cols 36-38 B). So the right segment of band D is a dead-end pocket.
- (27,21): D → (27,21) (rows 30-32, cols 21-23 are all B! confirmed above). So the vertical at cols 21-23 is broken at rows 30-32.
- (15,21): D → (27,21). So the vertical at cols 21-23 spans rows 15-29 (bands A, connector 18-20, band B 21-23, band C 27-29) — wait, from (15,21) D ends at (27,21): the vertical at cols 21-23 is continuous from rows 15 to 29.
So the "long vertical at cols 21-23" I imagined (rows 27-47) is actually two separate segments: rows 15-29 and rows 33-47 (the bottom one). The bottom segment (rows 33-47, cols 21-23) is only reachable from band D (rows 33-35) — which is itself unreachable.
So under slide semantics, the reachable region is the upper maze (11 states), and the bottom floor + goal is sealed off. Under 1-cell movement, everything is connected.
Therefore the actual movement rule must be 1-cell-per-press... but the RIGHT probe moved 6 cells in one step!
Unless... the RIGHT action in the history wasn't a single environment step. Wait: history entry 4: action RIGHT, frame step 4. Entry 3: LEFT, step 3. So each history entry = 1 step. The sprite moved 6 cells in one step.
Hmm, wait, maybe I'm misreading the sprite's position. Entry 3 (step 3): blue cells (15,15),(15,16),(15,17). Entry 4 (step 4): (15,21),(15,22),(15,23). Yes, 6 cells in one step.
So the movement is multi-cell per press. And slide-to-endpoint is unsolvable. Contradiction.
New hypothesis: the sprite slides until blocked, but the blocking check is done only on the center cell (1x1 collision)? Let me test: from (15,15) [center (16,16)], RIGHT: center moves right while cell(16,c) is passable. Row 16: cols 17 W, 18 g, 19 g, 20 g, 21 b→(now W), 22, 23, then col 24 B. Center stops at col 23? But the sprite's top-left ended at col 21, so center is (16,22). If center-only collision, center should stop at col 23 (col 24 is B). It stopped at 22. So not center-only.
Hypothesis: collision on the leading-edge column/row, but only on the center cell of that edge? For RIGHT: leading edge = right column (rows 15-17, col+2). Center of the right edge = (16, col+2). Stop when (16, col+3) is B? From (15,15): right-edge center (16,17); next (16,18) g OK... moves until (16,23) is the right-edge center and (16,24) B → top-left col 21. That matches! But this is the same as 3x3 box collision in this case, because the B at cols 24-26 spans all 3 rows.
The difference between "3x3 box" and "edge-center only" matters when the wall is partial (only 1 or 2 of the 3 rows). Are there partial walls in the maze? The sealing walls are full 3-row bands. So no difference.
OK, so let me think about this from a completely different angle. What if the game isn't "the sprite moves"? What if the arrow keys move the maze/camera, or shift the goal? No — the sprite clearly moved.
What if the sprite slides until blocked, and the block is determined by the next cell in the direction of motion for each of the 3 rows — i.e., same as box. Yes.
What if the sprite can pass through gray 'g' but g cells are "one-way" or "crumble"? No evidence.
Let me look at the maze design again. The upper region has 11 slide states — a nice little slide puzzle. The bottom floor is sealed off. Why would the designer make a sealed-off bottom floor with the goal in it? Maybe... the goal isn't the green box! Maybe the green box is a "portal" or "exit" and the real goal is something else. Or the green box is a decoration and the goal is to return the sprite to a specific spot?
Or: maybe the level is completed when the sprite reaches a position adjacent to the green box? Still unreachable.
Or: maybe the magenta bar at the bottom is a timer, and the goal is to survive? No.
Wait — maybe I should reconsider: the sprite's slide stops at the end of a corridor, and corridors are 3 wide... what if the sprite's box is actually 3 wide but the passability of 'g' differs from 'W' in terms of stopping: e.g., the sprite slides on W and stops at g (treats g as a "soft" stop)? Test: from (15,15) RIGHT: col 18 is g. If it stops at g, it should end at (15,15) (can't enter col 18). It moved to 21. So no.
What if the sprite moves exactly 6 cells per press (fixed)? Then from (15,21) RIGHT: 6 cells → cols 27-29? But cols 24-26 are B — it would overlap the wall. Unless it stops at the wall: min(6, distance to wall) = 6? Distance to wall from col 23 (right edge) to col 24 = 0 → can't move. Hmm, fixed-6 with wall clamp: from (15,21), RIGHT clamps to wall → stays. From (15,15): 6 cells → (15,21). That matches the probe! Fixed 6-cell movement with wall clamping is consistent with the probe!
But 6 is weird. Unless the move distance is "until wall" — same thing here.
Let me test the two hypotheses with a discriminating probe: from (15,21), press DOWN.
- Slide hypothesis: D from (15,21) → (27,21) (vertical at cols 21-23, rows 15-29, stop at B at rows 30-32).
- Fixed-6 hypothesis: D 6 cells → top-left (21,21)? Rows 21-23, cols 21-23: row 21 cols 21-23 = B! So clamped: how far down can it go? Rows 18-20 g (OK), rows 21-23 B → max move = 3 (to (18,21))? With fixed-6 clamped to wall: (18,21). With slide: (27,21).
These differ! Probe DOWN from (15,21): if sprite ends at rows 27-29 → slide confirmed; if rows 18-20 → fixed/clamped move.
Actually wait, I already have this data: from (15,21), the slide BFS predicted D → (27,21). But I haven't actually executed DOWN from (15,21). The history had UP at step 1 (from (15,15), no move — wall above, consistent with both).
Let me execute DOWN now and observe. This is the key discriminating probe.
Actually, let me also reconsider "slide but stop at junctions": from (15,21) D: first junction is at (21,21)? Band B rows 21-23, cols 21-23 is B — no. The vertical at cols 21-23: rows 15-17 W (band A), 18-20 g, 21-23 W (band B), 24-26 g, 27-29 W (band C), 30-32 B. Junctions along the way: at (18,21)? No horizontal corridor at rows 18-20 (only the vertical g). At (21,21): band B has a horizontal corridor (rows 21-23, cols 18-47) — junction! At (27,21): band C horizontal (rows 27-29, cols 21-35) — junction. If the sprite stops at the first junction, D from (15,21) → (21,21). If it slides to the end: (27,21).
So the DOWN probe discriminates three hypotheses:
- (21,21): stop at junction
- (27,21): slide to end
- (18,21): fixed/clamped 3? (fixed 6 clamped to wall at rows 21-23 B → 3 cells)
Let me execute DOWN and check.
